domain: Historical Theology / Ecclesiastical Authority / Commitment Systems
topic_summary: Analysis of the Filioque controversy: the unilateral Western addition of 'and the Son' to the Nicene Creed's pneumatology article ('the Spirit proceeds from the Father'), examining how competing readings of the 381 creed instantiate structurally divergent constraints on doctrinal authority, conciliar consent, and ecclesial unity.

key_entities: Roman See / Latin West (unilateral amender; magisterial authority claimant)
Eastern Churches / Constantinople (mono-procession defender; conciliar consent guardian)
key_tensions: Papal magisterial competence vs conciliar consent requirement (Western single-authority vs Eastern collegial-authority models)
Pneumatological theology vs ecclesiological authority structure (doctrinal content dispute overlaying institutional power dispute)

Filioque cited as 1054 schism cause, but structural entanglement with papal claims, liturgical differences, political fragmentation suggests overdetermined break. Single-cause narrative may be post-hoc legitimation.

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed (381 CE), specifically the pneumatology article: 'And [we believe] in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and Giver of Life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshiped and glorified.' This formula is the stabilized shared commitment.
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Interpretive legitimacy grounded in two competing models: (1) Western: papal magisterium and regional councils possess competence to clarify implicit doctrine (Filioque as legitimate development); (2) Eastern: only ecumenical councils of undivided Church possess amendment authority (Filioque as illegitimate unilateralism).
commitment_system_recognition.candidate_pattern: Pattern 3: Interpretive Monopoly Capture — Western reading grants Roman see exclusive interpretive authority over creedal meaning, generating high extractiveness (beneficiary: papal magisterium; victim: autocephalous Eastern churches whose consent is overridden). Pattern contested by Eastern wall-type constraint asserting ecumenical council monopoly.

readings.commitment: The Spirit proceeds from Father and Son (Filioque); papal/conciliar magisterium possesses authority to clarify implicit Trinitarian doctrine
readings.authority_grounding: Roman magisterial competence; regional councils (Toledo, Lateran); papal ratification
readings.expected_structural_delta: Anchor-type CS: fixes doctrinal unity under centralized Roman authority; beneficiary papal see; victim Eastern churches whose theological autonomy overridden; high ε (structural reconfiguration of ecclesial polity)

readings.commitment: The Spirit proceeds from Father alone; 381 creed inviolable without ecumenical consent; unilateral amendment constitutes breach
readings.authority_grounding: Ecumenical council exclusivity; conciliar consent requirement; principle of canonical autocephaly
readings.expected_structural_delta: Wall-type CS: blocks any single see from legislating doctrine for whole Church; beneficiary Eastern autocephalous churches; victim Western unilateral innovators; high ε (preserves decentralized polity structure)

readings.commitment: Both Filioque and mono-procession acceptable as regional theological expressions within single communion; bilateral recognition replaces unilateral imposition
readings.authority_grounding: Mutual recognition of valid local tradition; theological dialogue commissions; 20th-century ecumenical movement
readings.expected_structural_delta: Scaffold-type CS: permits theological pluralism under ecclesial unity; beneficiary ecumenical advocates; no direct victim set (consensus model); low-mod ε (coordination framework without coercive enforcement)

axiom_contradictions.basis: Filioque reading's axiom that papal magisterium possesses competence to clarify doctrine unilaterally is mutually exclusive with monoprocession reading's axiom that only ecumenical councils possess amendment authority. No coherent ecclesiology holds both: either a single see can bind the whole Church doctrinally (centralized magisterium) or it cannot (conciliar consent requirement). These are competing sovereignty models.

Reunion reading's axiom that regional theological diversity is permissible within communion contradicts Filioque reading's axiom that doctrinal uniformity under papal magisterium is necessary for ecclesial unity. One permits pluralism; the other requires conformity to a single magisterial interpretation.

Reunion reading's axiom of bilateral recognition (both formulae valid) contradicts monoprocession reading's axiom that the unmodified 381 creed is exclusively legitimate and Filioque constitutes breach. One treats amendment as acceptable regional expression; the other treats it as canonical violation requiring repudiation.
